items.title: Announcing MCP support in Apigee hybrid: agentic tools that run in your own cluster
items.summary: Apigee hybrid 1.17.0 introduces native Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, enabling the MCP data plane to run directly within your own Kubernetes cluster. This architecture ensures that AI agent request traffic and tool execution remain entirely inside your infrastructure while pulling configuration updates from the control plane. Developers can expose OpenAPI 3.0.x specifications as discoverable MCP tools, leverage existing security policies and API products, and trace end-to-end requests using W3C trace context headers.

items.title: Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
items.summary: This post announces native PyTorch backends for vLLM and SGLang powered by TorchTPU, enabling developers to run and optimize serving workloads using familiar PyTorch tools. Built in collaboration with open-source project maintainers, these engines include optimized TPU kernel implementations, production-ready features like KV cache management with TPU Sync, and disaggregated serving. Public benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and industry-leading cost efficiency on Ironwood TPU across long-context and agentic workloads.

items.title: Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
items.summary: Google Workspace now offers native support for Markdown (.md) files, allowing developers and AI agents to seamlessly collaborate on documentation directly in Google Docs without manual file conversions. This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.

items.title: Building Conversational Commerce with Multi-Agent Swarms on GCP: A Working Prototype
items.summary: This document provides a publication template and metadata structure for a technical blog post focused on building Conversational User Interfaces (CUIs) using AI. It outlines key developer focus areas, product stacks, and approval workflows required for publishing technical content through Google Developer Studio. The framework helps engineers organize their guides and solutions to effectively share AI-driven conversational interface designs with the developer community.

items.title: Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents
items.summary: See Google A2Ui in action! Learn how to natively render agentic UIs across Langchain, AWS Strands, Microsoft agents, and Google ADK using CopilotKit SDKs for A2UI.

items.title: Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond
items.summary: The Agents CLI Extension System enables developers to use frameworks like LangChain, LangGraph, or custom enterprise stacks while retaining a unified deployment and evaluation workflow. It details a first-party LangChain template that scaffolds, runs, and deploys agents without requiring the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Additionally, it demonstrates how platform teams can author custom extensions to enforce policies such as automated software bill of materials (SBOM) scans during deployment.

items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
items.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

items.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
items.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. These updates require no changes to frontend renderers or component catalogs, offering flexible performance levers for generative UI development across Python, TypeScript, and Dart.

Developers can use streaming tools to yield progress updates or background execution patterns to keep conversations fluid during long-running backend queries. items.title: Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer

items.title: Announcing DPoP Support for Google OAuth: Securing Refresh Tokens
items.summary: Google OAuth Platform now supports DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession) to sender-constrain refresh tokens, neutralizing Infostealer malware and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. By cryptographically binding long-lived refresh tokens while maintaining short-lived access tokens as standard Bearer tokens, developers achieve robust credential security without incurring high-QPS API performance overhead. Additionally, developers integrating multi-agent or Model Context Protocol (MCP) workloads can use Google Cloud Secure Token Service (STS) to handle secure token delegation across agent chains.

items.title: Morse Code Timing: The Hidden Math Behind Dots, Dashes, and the Farnsworth Method
items.summary: Morse Code Timing: The Hidden Math Behind Dots, Dashes, and the Farnsworth Method If you've ever tried to build a Morse code feature — a translator widget, a practice app, a hardware keyer — you've discovered that the "code" part is trivial. It's a lookup table. The hard part is the timing. Get the timing wrong and your decoder produces garbage, your audio sounds drunk, and your users quietly leave. This post is the timing reference I wish I'd had: the exact ratios, the WPM math, and the Farnsworth method that makes learning actually work. International Morse code timing is defined by the ITU, and it all derives from one unit: the dit (dot) duration. Everything else is a multiple of it: Dit = 1 unit Dah (dash) = 3 units Gap between dits/dahs within a character = 1 unit Gap between characters = 3 units Gap between words = 7 units That's it. Five rules, one unit. But the consequences are surprisingly deep. Take the letter A (.-). Its total duration is: 1 (dit) + 1 (intra-character gap) + 3 (dah) = 5 units. The word SOS (... --- ...) is: (1+1+1+1+1) + 3 + (3+1+3+1+3) + 3 + (1+1+1+1+1) = 27 units. Once you internalize the unit system, you can compute the duration of any message before

items.summary: Every time you close your MacBook lid on battery or unplug your display to walk to a meeting, macOS enters clamshell sleep. items.title: Obfuscating a .NET Worker Service: protecting a headless background worker
items.summary: A Worker Service is the quiet case in the obfuscation conversation. It has no controllers, no views, no public API that callers depend on — it is a BackgroundService on a timer, or an IHostedService draining a queue, built on the Generic Host and installed as a Windows Service or a systemd unit. Because it has no surface, two things are true at once: it is the easiest kind of .NET app to obfuscate aggressively, because almost nothing in it is observed by name, and it is the easiest to forget, because "it's just a background job on our customer's server" feels like it isn't exposed. It is exposed. This post is about treating a headless worker as what it is — a DLL in someone else's hands — and protecting it with the grain of the Generic Host rather than against it. The thing that makes a worker a tempting target is exactly what makes it feel safe: it has no front end. In a desktop or web app, a lot of the code is presentation, plumbing and framework glue, and the valuable logic is a fraction of it. A worker is almost all valuable logic. items.summary: ZUGFeRD-csharp is the open-source .NET library most teams use to create and read ZUGFeRD, Factur-X and XRechnung invoices (about 1.7 million NuGet downloads). Its maintainer has announced that maintenance ends on 30 November 2026. Until then there are only selected bug fixes and security reviews. After that the NuGet packages are marked as legacy and the repository is archived. New features and new standard versions go only into a commercial successor. Nothing breaks on 1 December: version 18.0.1 keeps working, and its Apache 2.0 licence stays. The risk is the next rule change. The rules for German and French e-invoices are updated several times a year. KoSIT's last XRechnung configuration came out on 31 August 2026, and the French reform's rules are still moving. And from 1 January 2027, German companies with more than €800,000 turnover in the previous year must send e-invoices to German business customers. So if your .NET app writes invoices with ZUGFeRD-csharp, here are the four ways forward I see, with what each costs you. The cheapest option, and a sensible one for now. items.title: I built 26 PDF and image tools that run entirely on your device
items.summary: I got tired of a very small, very specific kind of annoyance. You need to do something simple. Shrink a photo so it will actually send. Sort out a PDF before you email it. You find an app, open it, and before it does anything it wants you to create an account. Or it quietly sends your file off to a server somewhere, does the work there, and sends it back. items.title: Cron Job Scheduling for Node.js Recurring Reminders: Idempotent Retry Control
items.summary: Short answer: schedule the recurring reminder as a durable work item, then let a rate-limited worker claim it with an idempotency key. Cron should create due work; it should not be the delivery system. That separation matters in customer support. A reminder such as ticket-4821: ask for an update can be due at 09:00, but the notification service may be full, the provider may return a retryable error, or two scheduler instances may notice the same due row. The correct outcome is one reminder, eventually delivered, with a retry history that an on-call engineer can inspect. The practical rule is small: retries may repeat attempts, never the business effect. That is the boundary. The scheduler should write or upsert a work record keyed by the business event, for example ticket-4821/2026-10-24T09:00:00Z. A unique constraint on that key turns overlapping cron runs into a harmless race. The worker then claims the record for a bounded lease and passes the same idempotency key on every attempt. This is different from putting a sendReminder() call directly in a cron callback. A process restart can happen after the remote system accepts the notification but before the callback records success.

We are told to memorize that a /26 prefix provides 62 usable hosts, that 255.255.255.192 corresponds to a block size of 64, or that 192.168.1.130 falls into the second subnet. items.title: The same snippet in Bun and in a browser
items.summary: "Universal JavaScript" sounds simple until your helper touches document, process or fs. Here's a quick way to sort what's portable from what isn't, and a pattern for the bits that aren't. A surprising amount of the platform is the same in Bun and in a browser page. All of this runs unchanged in both: const url = new URL("https://example.com/search?q=bun&page=2"); url.searchParams.get("page"); // "2" const copy = structuredClone(new Map([["a", { n: 1 }]])); copy.get("a"); // { n: 1 } new TextEncoder().encode("héllo").length; // 6 bytes, 5 characters new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat("en", { numeric: "auto" }).format(-1, "day"); // "yesterday" crypto.randomUUID().length; // 36 URL, structuredClone, TextEncoder, Intl, crypto.randomUUID, fetch, setTimeout, AbortController: if your helper sticks to these, it's portable already. Run these three lines and the answers depend on where you are: "document" in globalThis; "Bun" in globalThis; globalThis.process?.versions?.bun ?? items.title: MIT Researchers Used GPT-6 Astra To Edit Qwen's Open Weights Directly, Boosting Math Scores
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from VentureBeat: Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) reported today that they used OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra language model to raise a small, open source Qwen model's math score roughly sixfold by directly editing its weights -- the numerical parameters that govern its behavior. Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab described their work in a research blog post published November 2. They call the approach "weight-space programming" and tested Astra's ability to interpret and alter networks without using conventional training procedures to generate the edits. In the strongest language-model example, Astra's intervention raised Qwen3.5-0.8B's MATH-500 score from 7.9% to 48.1% while touching approximately 0.016% of its weights. The improvement came primarily from correcting repetitive reasoning—a distinction that shaped both the technical findings and the debate over their implications. items.summary: Originally published on munchymatess.app. Desktop pets are an old idea. Little characters that walk along your windows have been around since the early days of Windows, and the Japanese Shimeji made them famous with fans drawing their own characters. Search for a desktop pet for Mac today and you'll find plenty that do the same thing: they walk, they climb, they sit on your windows. That's cute for a day. Then you stop noticing them. A pet that does the same thing whatever you're doing is a screensaver with legs. The pets people keep for months have one thing in common: they notice your Mac. Here's what that means, what to look for, and how I built it into Munchy Mates. Your Mac already knows a lot about your day. It knows how much battery is left, whether the charger is in, what time it is, whether you're on a call or in Focus, and which file you just dragged. A pet that reads those things can respond to your day, which is what makes it feel alive. In Munchy Mates, your battery is the pet's lunchbox. At 20% she gets hungry. At 10% she's in tears. items.title: How to Catch PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy and Required-Reason API Gaps Before App Store Submission
items.summary: Apple's privacy-manifest requirements have added a new release checklist for iOS teams. A repository can contain app-owned code that uses a Required-Reason API, one or more PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy files, and third-party SDKs that have their own privacy-manifest or signature requirements. The painful time to discover an obvious gap is after preparing a release. This guide shows a bounded, repeatable way to check repository evidence before App Store Connect upload. It does not replace Apple's final build validation or App Review. For a privacy-manifest preflight, three questions are especially useful: Does app-owned native source contain signals for Apple's Required-Reason API categories? Do the scanned PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy files appear to cover those categories without obvious structure gaps? Do dependency files contain SDKs on Apple's commonly used SDK list that deserve version-specific privacy-manifest/signature review? Common App Store Connect messages developers search for include ITMS-91053 and ITMS-91056. items.title: Central package management and feature flags solve the same problem at opposite speeds
items.summary: I keep seeing the same argument in microservice estates, and it usually gets framed as a tooling choice. Should we pin every NuGet version in one place with central package management, or lean on feature flags so each service can ship new behaviour whenever it likes? Wrong framing. They don't compete. They control two different kinds of change, and most of the pain I see comes from using one to do the other's job. Here is the split. Central package management, the Directory.Packages.props file with ManagePackageVersionsCentrally switched on, decides what code is compiled into your binaries. A feature flag decides which compiled code runs right now. One acts at build time, the other at runtime. Obvious when stated that way, and yet teams routinely try to roll out a risky library upgrade by hiding it behind a flag, which can't work. Why not? Because the flag can't un-load an assembly. If service A upgrades a shared client library from 4.x to 5.x, the 5.x types are in the process whether the flag is on or off. Static initialisers run. Transitive dependencies get resolved. items.title: Your AI Agent Can Write SwiftUI That Compiles on Mac, iPhone, and iPad — and Still Get All Three Wrong
items.summary: Ask an AI coding agent to build a settings screen in SwiftUI, and it'll hand you something that compiles everywhere Apple ships a screen — iPhone, iPad, Mac, even Vision Pro. That's not the hard part anymore. Getting an LLM to produce SwiftUI that builds across Apple platforms is almost table stakes in 2026. Getting it to look like it belongs on each of those platforms is a completely different problem, and it's one that doesn't show up as a red squiggle anywhere. Run that agent-written settings screen on iPad and you get a phone layout stretched into a wider window. Run it on Mac and there's no sidebar, no menu-bar affordances, nothing that reads as "a Mac app" instead of "an iPhone app someone recompiled." The code is correct. It compiles, it runs, nothing crashes. It's just wrong in a way that only shows up if a human actually opens it on the other two devices — which an agent, working from a single mental model of "the app," has no particular reason to do unless you force it to. This is the part of "AI writes your UI now" that gets glossed over. items.title: What a killed Playwright script leaves behind on Linux: processes, profile dirs and a SIGTERM that does not exit
items.summary: A Playwright script ends in more ways than await browser.close(): it throws, someone calls process.exit(), a container runtime sends SIGTERM, the OOM killer sends SIGKILL. I wanted to know what each of these leaves behind on a Linux host: running Chromium processes, temp directories, or a Node process that ignores the signal. I ran all of it on 2026-11-03: Linux 6.8, Node v24.22.2, Playwright 1.63.0 with the bundled chrome-headless-shell (revision 1243). Everything below is that one machine and one browser build. Containers, systemd, macOS and Windows are not covered. The child script launches a browser, opens a page, prints READY, and then either waits for a GO line on stdin and ends in a chosen way, or hangs so that the harness can send it a signal. items.summary: I have been building a unit converter for iOS since 2016 (convertunits.app). Late 2025 I rewrote it in SwiftUI. Then Apple announced the iPhone Duo, and I had about six weeks to make the app look right on a device I could only run in the Xcode 27.1 simulator. Two weeks after launch, 824 of my existing users had restored the app on a Duo. This post covers what broke, the code that fixed it, and how I counted those users, since App Store Connect does not list the Duo as a device. Folded, the outer display is a little wider than an iPhone (466 × 678 pt) and compact width. The status bar is not at the top: it sits in a column on the right edge, so the top safe area inset is close to zero and the right one carries everything. Unfolded in landscape, the inner display is 951 × 669 pt, regular × regular, with an 84 pt status column on the right and nothing on the left. The fold crosses the display at its physical middle, x = 475.5 pt, which is not the middle of the safe area. Every bug below comes from one of those three facts: the top inset is gone, the screen is suddenly wide, and the insets are asymmetric. items.title: What I learned from building a relational database engine in C#
items.summary: I’ve used Microsoft SQL Server for decades without ever seeing how it works inside. Sure, there’s ample documentation, but reading it isn’t the same thing as looking at the implementation code. Since the source is closed, I did the next best thing: I built my own relational database engine in C#, to face the same problems it must solve. Today, my engine supports transactions, concurrency, and crash recovery. It also has a management tool. It can run both in-process and as a server, and I now rely on it in my daily work. For instance, my company’s invoicing goes through it. I studied databases at university, and textbooks explain B-trees, SQL parsing, ACID principles, transactions, and recovery well. What they don’t show is how those pieces interact when something goes wrong at the worst possible moment. I quickly noticed that this was the thing left out of those books. And quite naturally, this led to the next question: what testing methods are needed to support this kind of work? In this post, I wanted to share the lessons I learned. items.title: Migrating from Homegrown License Keys to Keyright Without Breaking Customers
items.summary: Every homegrown licensing system starts the same way: a weekend, a GUID, a checksum, maybe a little XOR "encryption," and a check that returns true. It ships, it works, and then it quietly becomes load-bearing. Years later you want real seats, online activation, revocation and a customer portal — and you hit the question that stops most teams cold: how do I move thousands of customers already running keys in the field onto a proper system without a flag day, a mass reactivation email, and a week of support tickets? You can, and no customer needs to notice. The trick is to treat the migration as a transition window rather than a switch, and to make the client read both formats while you quietly re-issue proper licenses underneath. This post is the concrete plan. Key takeaway: Migrate behind one interface. Ship a client that validates the new signed license first and falls back to your legacy key, issue a signed license for every existing customer from your own records, deliver it like any update, and let each app switch itself over silently on next launch. items.title: PM2 vs systemd for Node.js in Production: Which Should You Use? (2026)
items.summary: Every Node.js app on a VPS needs something to start it, restart it when it crashes and bring it back after a reboot. The two common answers are PM2 and systemd. Both work. They're good at different things. PM2 if you want cluster mode, pm2 reload with no dropped requests, and friendly per-app commands. systemd if you want zero extra dependencies, strict sandboxing and the same tool you use for every other service. systemd is the init system on almost every modern Linux distro. It already runs Nginx, SSH and cron. A Node app becomes one more unit file. PM2 is a Node.js process manager installed via npm. It runs its own daemon, which manages your apps and is itself started by systemd through pm2 startup. ShipOwn's guide What Is PM2? covers it in depth. items.title: Role-based access to reports and folders in ASP.NET Core: users, roles and admin claims
items.summary: By Razi Syed. Sample code: github.com/dotnetreport/dotnetreport-multitenant-rls Once users can build and save their own reports, a second question shows up almost immediately: who gets to see which report? Finance wants a "Payroll by department" report that the rest of the company never sees. A team lead wants to share one report with their team, read-only. Support wants a handful of people to be able to fix everybody's broken reports. And someone has to be able to change the reporting schema itself, which is a very different permission from "can edit a report". If you model all of that as one IsAdmin flag, you end up either locking users out of the thing you built for them, or handing everyone the keys. This article walks through how I separate those concerns in ASP.NET Core using the role and claim hooks in Dotnet Report (which I work on — disclosure). The pattern carries over even if you build your own report builder: identity comes from the server, permissions are data on each report and folder, and admin powers are claims, checked on the server. items.title: Your Node API isn't slow. It's waiting for a database connection.
items.summary: It's fine in testing. Then 200 people open the same page at once and the endpoint takes ten seconds. CPU is flat. Postgres says every query is fast. Nothing looks slow, and yet everything is stuck. That shape usually means requests are queuing for a database connection, not for compute. This post covers why it happens in Node, how to spot it, the fixes (with code), and how to prove the fix worked. One write-up on dev.to describes a NestJS admin dashboard on Postgres. A stress test fired 200 identical dashboard requests at a 250k-entry ledger through a pool of 5 connections. The first run came back with a p95 of 9.8 seconds. Each load held eight pooled connections: one query for the money cards and six separate statements for queue counts, all recomputed per request even though the 200 requests asked for the same thing. After the fix (coalescing identical in-flight requests and collapsing six queue-count queries into one), p95 dropped to 213 ms with zero errors, and connections per load fell from eight to three. items.title: An AVIF quality ladder in sharp: q30 to q80, bytes and time
items.summary: In sharp, AVIF bytes grow fast with quality: a 1920 × 1280 photo of 576.8 KB came out at 54.4 KB at q30, 119.0 KB at q50 (sharp's default) and 332.7 KB at q80. That is 6.1 times the bytes from the bottom of the ladder to the top. Encode time stayed between 0.6 and 1.2 seconds on an M1 Pro at the default effort. The script, run from a folder with sharp installed: import sharp from 'sharp'; import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'; const input = await readFile('jpg-sample-photo-original.jpg'); const median = (a) => [...a].sort((x, y) => x - y)[Math.floor(a.length / 2)]; await sharp(input).avif({ quality: 50 }).toBuffer(); // warm-up console.log('quality bytes KB ms(median of 5)'); for (const q of [30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80]) { const times = []; let bytes = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { const t = performance.now(); const out = await sharp(input).avif({ quality: q }).toBuffer(); times.push(performance.now() - t); bytes = out.length; } console.log(`q${q}`.padEnd(9), String(bytes).padEnd(8), (bytes / 1000).toFixed(1).padEnd(7), median(times).toFixed(0)); } What it printed: quality bytes KB ms(median of 5) q30 54361 54.4 980 q40 80292 80.3 624 q50 118975 119.0 711 q60 172876 172.9 779

items.title: Stop trusting your AGENTS.md: the drift-check that makes it a contract
items.summary: Back in September I published Stop bloating your AGENTS.md: reference your conventions instead of pasting them — and advice I still stand behind: keep AGENTS.md a thin index, move the details into per-topic docs, reference them from one place. The argument was about context hygiene — your conventions stay detailed, your context stays clean. What that argument never claimed to do was enforcement. It was a solid argument. It was also half an argument, and the second half bit me within two weeks of real agent work. Because here's the uncomfortable truth I glossed over: a lean AGENTS.md is still just prose. ESLint enforces boundaries because CI turns red. AGENTS.md enforces itself because... nothing does. The agent reads it, nods, and the next time a task touches an edge case the doc doesn't cover, the doc becomes fiction. It doesn't drift loudly. It drifts quietly, one merge at a time, until you open it a month later and realize it describes a codebase that doesn't exist. items.title: Fixing App Store Connect screenshot errors: wrong dimensions and alpha channels
items.summary: App Store Connect usually gives you two kinds of screenshot errors: the dimensions are wrong, or the file has an alpha channel. Both are quick to check from the terminal on a Mac before you upload anything. sips sips ships with macOS: for f in *.png; do sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight -g hasAlpha "$f" | tr '\n' ' '; echo done Compare the output with Apple's screenshot specifications. items.title: How to upload iPhone Duo screenshots in App Store Connect

Here's the manual upload workflow, plus the details that tend to trip people up. Neither Duo size shares an aspect ratio with a regular iPhone, so scaling your existing set won't give you valid files. Apple says Duo screenshots will be required for submissions starting April 2027, for apps built with the iOS 27.1 SDK or later. The SDK condition matters: read it before you plan around the date. Start from real captures of your app. Guideline 2.3.3 says screenshots must show the app in use, not just title art or marketing renders. items.summary: If you're running a React Router app in framework mode, you get SSR out of the box and for production it hands you @react-router/serve, a small server built on top of Express. While it does the job, Express carries a bit of history (and weight) with it, so if you're the kind of person who wants a leaner server, or just more control over what happens around your app, there's a really nice alternative that drops in with almost no glue. The createRequestHandler from react-router gives you a function that takes a standard web Request and resolves to a standard web Response, that's the whole contract. It doesn't care about Node, Express, or any particular server, it just wants a Request and it'll give you back a Response. Hono is built on those exact same web standards and, inside its handler, context.req.raw is already a web Request. This means that passing a request from Hono to React Router is basically one line, with no conversions, no bridging and no fuss. Since Hono itself doesn't listen on a port, it's just a handler, to actually run it on Node you'll have to bring in @hono/node-server, whose serve function takes your app.fetch and wires it up to Node's built-in http server. items.title: Telr payments in ASP.NET Core: the parts the docs skip
items.summary: Telr’s hosted payment page takes an afternoon to wire up. The real work is everything around it: the redirect that never comes back, the callback that arrives twice, and the payment that lands after you already released the seats. With a hosted payment page your API never touches the card. You create an order at Telr, send the customer to the page it returns, and wait to hear how it went. You hear it three ways, and they are not equal. The return URL. The browser comes back to your authorised, declined or cancelled page. Useful for the user, worthless as proof: anyone can type that URL, and a closed tab never arrives at all. The callback. Telr posts a signed, form-encoded advice to your server (ivp_update_url). Good evidence once you check the signature, but it can arrive late, twice, or before the browser does. order/check. Your server asks Telr about the order by its reference. This is the answer you act on, and the one to fall back to whenever the other two disagree or go quiet. A double click on Pay, a retry from a flaky phone connection, two tabs: all of them ask for a second payment session for the same order. Two live sessions means a customer can pay twice. items.summary: SignalR com .NET 10: implementando comunicação em tempo real na prática Em muitas aplicações, precisamos atualizar informações no front-end assim que um evento acontece no back-end. Imagine um sistema de processamento de pedidos. Quando um pagamento é aprovado, o usuário precisa ser notificado imediatamente, sem atualizar a página. Embora funcione, essa estratégia pode gerar requisições desnecessárias, aumentar o consumo de recursos e introduzir latência entre o processamento de um evento e sua visualização. É justamente nesse cenário que o ASP.NET Core SignalR se destaca. Neste artigo, vamos entender como o SignalR funciona e implementar uma aplicação de notificações em tempo real utilizando .NET 10, Minimal APIs e JavaScript. items.title: JavaScript SEO FAQ: 11 questions frontend devs ask (with straight answers)
items.summary: Every frontend team ends up having the same SEO conversation, usually right after marketing asks why the new React site gets less search traffic than the old WordPress one. Here are the questions that come up most often, with straight answers and code where it helps. Yes. Googlebot renders pages with an evergreen Chromium. But rendering happens in a second stage: the raw HTML is crawled first, and rendering is queued. For most sites the delay is short, but anything that exists only after rendering gets discovered later and less reliably than content in the initial HTML. Other crawlers (many social preview bots, some search engines, plenty of SEO and AI tools) don't execute JavaScript at all. Practical answer: put critical content and links in the server-rendered HTML when you can. need SSR or static generation? Not strictly. Client-rendered apps can rank. But SSR or SSG removes a whole class of problems: slow rendering, render failures, missing meta tags for non-JS crawlers. If the pages are meant to rank (marketing, docs, product, blog), pre-render them. If it's a logged-in dashboard, don't bother. items.title: Opening hours component in React with time zones
items.summary: The first "Open now" badge I shipped for a client lied. The salon was in Zurich, the site was deployed on servers in the US, and I was testing from my laptop at home. It showed "Open" at 11 pm because somewhere in the chain a date was created in the wrong time zone. That bug is the reason the Opening hours component and the Open now badge in Facade compute everything in the business's own IANA time zone and never trust the raw clock. Here is how they work. new Date() gives you the visitor's local time. A visitor in Los Angeles looking at a barber in New York gets a Date whose getHours() is three hours behind the shop. Compare that to the shop's hours and the badge is wrong for every out of town visitor, which on a site that ranks for the city name is most of them. The server is no better. On Vercel or any cloud host the server clock is UTC or whatever region the function runs in. If you render "Open now" on the server, you render it in the server's zone, and the first paint in the browser disagrees with the hydrated one. items.title: Prompt packs for empty / error / loading states — stop shipping happy-path only
items.summary: Agents are weirdly good at the happy path. Give them a Figma frame of a filled dashboard and you get a filled dashboard. Give them a “build a projects list” prompt and you get rows, avatars, and a neat toolbar. What you usually don’t get: the empty list on day one, the 500 that lands mid-scroll, or the skeleton that doesn’t jump when real data arrives. Those states are where users decide whether the product feels finished — and they’re the first thing agents skip unless you ask for them on purpose. So I stopped describing “the screen” and started shipping prompt packs for the three non-happy states every surface needs. For any list / detail / settings panel the agent touches, I keep a tiny markdown pack next to the feature (or in the PR description). Four required stories: Happy — data present, primary actions enabled Empty — zero rows / first-run / filtered-to-nothing (these are different) Error — failed fetch, partial failure, retry affordance Loading — initial load and refetch / pagination (also different) If the agent only returns #1, the PR is incomplete. items.title: TypeScript Email Fixtures That Fail Clearly
items.summary: Email verification tests often fail in the least helpful way: a button is clicked, a test waits, and then the runner reports a timeout. The product may be fine. The test may have created the wrong inbox. An old message may have won the race. Or the polling helper simply forgot to record what it saw. I like solving this at the fixture boundary. If a test needs to generate disposable email, the returned value should be more than a string. It should carry the inbox identity, the trigger time, and enough evidence to explain a miss. That makes a use and throw email address useful for a controlled test run without making the rest of the suite guess what happened. A basic helper usually looks harmless: const inbox = await createInbox(); await page.getByLabel("Email").fill(inbox.address); await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Create account" }).click(); await waitForEmail(inbox.address); The trouble starts when waitForEmail returns only a link or throws only TimeoutError. A retry can pass with a different message, while the original cause disappears. In a busy test suite, that is very hard to triage. "We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology," the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a blog post. The Register reports: Videostrong Technology is a hardware manufacturer based in Shenzhen, China. It builds Android devices, including home TV boxes and projectors. According to Google, Videostrong deliberately embedded the XCPE backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates, allowing them to install additional malware modules on devices shipped to unsuspecting customers. When buyers connected these devices to their home networks, the preinstalled backdoor allowed operators to create proxy networks and hide malicious traffic using the customers' internet connections without their knowledge. items.title: Next.js Cache Not Working? A 10-Step Checklist for Next.js 15 and 16
items.summary: Quick Summary You save some data. The database says yes. The page still shows the old data. If your Next.js cache is not working, Next.js is usually doing what you told it to do, just on an old copy of the page that you forgot about. A Next.js page can live in four places at once: the build, the server, the browser, and a CDN. Below are five quick questions and 10 steps in order. They help you find the old copy and fix it, for Next.js 15 and for the new use cache style in Next.js 16. Do not ask "is the cache broken?" Ask "which copy am I looking at?" Since Next.js 15, fetch is not cached by default. But a page built ahead of time can still keep old data from build day. revalidate does not mean "refresh every N seconds". The first visitor after the time is over still sees the old page. In Next.js 16, revalidateTag('x') with one argument is the old way. Use updateTag or revalidateTag('x', 'max'). Reloading the page fixes an old browser copy. It does nothing for the other three. People say "cache" like it is one thing. It is not. items.summary: At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, Chinese space officials publicly outlined the most detailed roadmap yet for landing astronauts on the Moon "before 2030." Ars Technica reports: China's lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon. According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves: - An uncrewed test of the Long March 10A rocket (a single-stick variant, with no boosters) and the Mengzhou spacecraft to low-Earth orbit. Target: early 2027 - An uncrewed test of the larger Long March 10 rocket (a core stage with two boosters) and the Lanyue lunar lander, including descent/ascent from Moon's surface. Target: 2028 - A concurrent launch of two Long March 10 rockets, one carrying uncrewed Mengzhou and the other the Lanyue vehicle; they will dock in lunar orbit. items.title: BYD Sold More EVs Last Month Than the US Did All Quarter
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Electrek: The world's leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company's highest monthly total in 2026. BYD's battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark. To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates. By the end of the year, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. "In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles," adds Electrek. Brave also promotes "hundreds of top publishers" as being accessible through its "Paywall blocker" feature in its browser. "Brave has never asked for the Publishers' permission to access their websites, much less to copy the material and provide it to users or other AI companies," the complaint says. "The company has confirmed problems across a chunk of its software estate, leaving some customers facing incorrect times, broken schedules and a collection of workarounds while Redmond catches up," reports The Register. From the report: Outlook users have been left with the most homework. Switching to the new Canadian time zones won't automatically update existing calendar entries, meaning that meetings scheduled after November 1 are potentially an hour out of whack. Microsoft advises users to change their Outlook calendar time zone, then update upcoming events and meetings to use it. For meetings involving other people, only the organizer can make the change. Recurring meetings come with an additional treat: changing the time zone resets any previously moved occurrences, which then have to be recreated. items.summary: Marvell has agreed to acquire optical components maker Lumentum in an all-stock deal with an implied enterprise value of $115 billion. "AI infrastructure is undergoing a fundamental architectural shift toward optical connectivity, creating an opportunity that comes along once in a generation," said Marvell Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy. "The companies that move first and help define this transition will set the standard for decades to come." CNBC reports: Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models. Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

Further down the list came “for future reference” and “kindly note”. If you ask me, these all verge on actual aggressive. Imagine saying “just to be clear” out loud to another person: that’s a conversational poke in the ribs, isn’t it? It’s the kind of thing you unleash 10 minutes into an ill-tempered wrangle with your home insurance company about inflated renewal premiums. “Kindly note” is even worse – it’s a phrase from an angry message on the office kitchen wall about microwave abuse. items.title: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?
items.summary: Using AI for roles from executive assistants to chiefs of staff, companies are boasting about doing more with less, creating tension with their human workers On an average workday, Dhruv Amin chats with dozens of colleagues to get things done at his AI startup Anything. He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen. But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. At Anything, there are 15 human employees and roughly 150 agents – a ratio that Amin believes will soon be the norm. Continue reading...

items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. items.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
items.summary: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago. Continue reading...
